title: WIP presentations
description: Works-in-progress presentations from Pete Hitchcock on a decision-science approach to negative self-judgment in depression and Michael Hallquist on learning what to choose and when to act, connecting response vigor, matching, and free-operant behavior, with time for discussion and feedback. presentations.title: Making Progress on Inherently Complex ("Low Essentiality") Disorders: A Case Study
presentations.description: Hitchcock introduces the idea that mental health problems vary in their inherent complexity and argues that depression and generalized anxiety are inherently complex, or low in essentiality. As a case study in making progress on these problems, he describes the lab’s decision-science approach to negative self-judgment in depression. This work builds on sequential-sampling models, in which decisions unfold by accumulating evidence over time: visual evidence for perceptual judgments, such as identifying a traffic light’s color, and personal value associations for food choices, such as choosing between Butterfingers and Reese’s.

presentations.title: Learning when to act and what to choose
presentations.description: Hallquist explores how learning shapes both action choice and response timing, connecting response vigor with the matching law. He compares computational models across reward schedules, extinction, changing reward environments, and tasks that reward waiting. The talk highlights where the models succeed and fall short, and proposes human studies to test their potential relevance to anhedonia, effort-related inactivity, and impulsive action.

title: Advancing cognitive behavioral theories and therapies with computational models
description: Don Robinaugh from Northeastern will give an EDM Zoom talk. Watch together in PAIS 280.
abstract: Cognitive behavioral theories of mental disorders have received considerable empirical support. However, these theories rarely develop over time in a way that would indicate a substantial accumulation of knowledge. Perhaps not surprisingly, then, the efficacy of cognitive behavioral treatments for many disorders has not improved in decades. In this talk, I will argue that formalizing cognitive behavioral theories as computational models is one means by which we might better advance our theories and our treatments. I will illustrate how computational models equip us to more accurately and precisely deduce what our theories predict, and how these advantages can be applied to advance our understanding of how treatments work, why they sometimes fail, and how they might be improved. Finally, I will discuss the challenges facing this work and the importance of integrating formalized clinical theory with computational models from other areas of psychology and psychiatry.
